key_insight: Machine-learned long-time simulations show that small polarons at oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110) surfaces move far more slowly than in the bulk because surface geometry removes many favorable hopping pathways.
engineering_relevance: The work explains why porous rutile TiO2 can have lower electron mobility than single-crystal material, informing surface engineering for catalysis, photovoltaics, batteries, and energy-storage devices.
method: Extended machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics to a reducible oxide surface
Simulated oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110) for several nanoseconds across temperatures
Analyzed hopping pathways, interlayer transfer, and vacancy-induced charge localization
evidence_signal: Nanosecond-scale dynamics reveal several-orders-of-magnitude lower surface polaron mobility than in bulk, with vacancies biasing electrons toward nearby Ti sites and only rare interlayer hops.
watch_item: The conclusions rely on a specific reduced TiO2(110) surface model, so transferability to other oxide surfaces and defect chemistries should be validated case by case.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
